article.title: OpenClaw Ships Its Largest-Ever Update, Adding Multiplayer 'Shared Cloud Sessions' as Security Critics Push Back
article.summary: OpenClaw 2.0 adds team-shared agent sessions and simpler onboarding, but reviewers note sandboxing and execution approvals still ship off by default.
article.body_markdown:
## Overview

OpenClaw, the open-source personal AI agent framework, has shipped version 2.0, which its maintainers call ["by far the largest update in the history of OpenClaw"](https://openclaw.ai/blog/openclaw-2-accidentally). The release, tagged [v2026.8.1](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/releases/tag/v2026.8.1), adds a new team-collaboration feature called shared cloud sessions and a redesigned installation flow, but reviewers at [VentureBeat](https://venturebeat.com/ai/openclaw-2-0-is-here-what-it-means-for-enterprises) and [The Register](https://www.theregister.com/ai-and-ml/2026/08/31/openclaw-20-pours-glitter-on-slow-burning-security-dumpster-fire/5293492) note that sandboxing and execution approvals still ship turned off by default, five months after a wave of critical vulnerabilities forced emergency patches across the project.

OpenClaw runs locally on a user's own hardware and connects to messaging platforms so people can delegate tasks to an autonomous AI agent. As [previously reported](/article/2026-03/11-openclaw-surpasses-react-as-githubs-most-starred-project-then-triggers-a-cascading-security-crisis), the project became the most-starred non-aggregator project on GitHub in March 2026, a rise that was quickly followed by a cascade of disclosed vulnerabilities, including a zero-click exploit called "ClawJacked," that exposed more than 135,000 publicly reachable instances.

## What We Know

### A release built by hundreds of contributors

According to the [official OpenClaw Foundation blog post](https://openclaw.ai/blog/openclaw-2-accidentally) announcing the update, "It was built by 933 contributors, including 569 first-time contributors, and is composed of over 16,000 pull requests." The post's author, Hannes Rudolph, the foundation's community manager, wrote that "going nearly seven weeks without shipping was not normal for us," noting that "before this update, we had shipped 106 releases in 230 days."

The blog post frames the update's priorities around three areas: installation, the browser interface, and multiplayer collaboration. On setup, the post says, "Installation was the first place we needed to make OpenClaw easier, so for first-time installs we are starting with what is already on someone's computer," letting new users lean on subscriptions and API keys they already hold rather than a lengthy configuration process.

### Shared cloud sessions bring teams into one workspace

The headline feature is "shared cloud sessions," which lets multiple people collaborate inside the same agent workspace rather than each running an isolated instance. [VentureBeat reports](https://venturebeat.com/ai/openclaw-2-0-is-here-what-it-means-for-enterprises) that OpenClaw creator Peter Steinberger said the team had been dogfooding the approach, noting "Two months ago, we started the mission to 'build OpenClaw with OpenClaw,'" gradually shifting from individual coding harnesses to shared team environments. One user identified as Colin described the effect on handoffs between teammates, saying "the session itself became the handoff document," according to VentureBeat.

VentureBeat also reports that the redesigned Control UI now prioritizes conversation as the primary interface, similar to ChatGPT or Claude, while still exposing the underlying technical detail — a shift aimed at broadening adoption beyond engineering teams.

Separately, the [GitHub release notes for v2026.8.1](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/releases/tag/v2026.8.1) list a set of features that support that collaborative workflow: conversation search that lets users "search visible conversation text by exact words or phrases and reopen the surrounding messages from a matching result," sessions that can run on cloud workers beyond a user's own machine, durable session progress cards, and a private-credential-request flow that lets an agent ask for a credential "without putting its value in chat or model context." The release notes also describe expanded media handling, adding "richer audio and video" with "native playback controls and video uploads on Apple and Android clients." GitHub shows 970 commits separating the release from the prior main branch.

The update also carries breaking changes: the OpenProse plugin has been removed, with users directed to run `openclaw doctor --fix` and follow migration documentation, and OpenAI model references must be updated from the `codex/*` and `openai-codex/*` prefixes to `openai/*`, per the GitHub release notes.

### Security defaults draw renewed scrutiny

The collaborative features have drawn scrutiny over security defaults. VentureBeat reports that "OpenClaw's documentation explicitly says sandboxing and execution approvals are off by default," and that the software's "baseline configuration assumes a trusted single operator and permits host execution unless administrators configure stronger restrictions." VentureBeat contrasts this with NanoClaw, a container-first alternative that "runs agents inside Docker containers, limits those containers to explicitly mounted filesystems and runs their processes as an unprivileged user."

[The Register](https://www.theregister.com/ai-and-ml/2026/08/31/openclaw-20-pours-glitter-on-slow-burning-security-dumpster-fire/5293492), in a piece headlined "OpenClaw 2.0 pours glitter on slow-burning security dumpster fire," reports separately that "Sandboxing is turned off by default" and that the new shared sessions lack "tenant isolation or a security boundary." The outlet also reports that the new Secret Store feature for handling credentials has its own limitation: "Secret Store values are not encrypted at rest and depend on the filesystem permissions."

## What We Don't Know

Neither the OpenClaw Foundation's blog post nor the GitHub release notes address the security criticisms raised by VentureBeat and The Register, so it is not clear whether default-off sandboxing and unencrypted-at-rest secret storage reflect a deliberate design tradeoff for usability or are slated to change in a future release. The foundation has not published a response to the specific critiques about tenant isolation in shared sessions.

## Analysis

OpenClaw's 2.0 release repeats a pattern the project has followed since its founding: rapid feature expansion aimed at making autonomous agents more accessible, paired with security defaults that trail behind that expansion. The March 2026 crisis emerged in large part because OpenClaw bound its gateway to all network interfaces by default and trusted local connections automatically — a convenience-over-security tradeoff similar in spirit to what reviewers are now flagging in shared cloud sessions and the Secret Store. Multiplayer collaboration on autonomous agents with file, credential, and execution access raises the stakes of any isolation gap, since a single compromised session could now expose work shared across an entire team rather than one individual's instance.
